Consult Summary:
- Adult with history of asthma and atopy presenting with 2–3 days of wheeze and exertional dyspnea; managed as asthma exacerbation with increased short-acting bronchodilator use, spacer/peak flow, antihistamine, and follow-up in 1 week.

History:
- Presenting complaint: 2–3 days of wheezing and shortness of breath.
- Associated symptoms: Dry cough; denies sputum and hemoptysis. Denies chest pain. Not waking at night. Dyspnea on walking; sometimes difficulty completing sentences; can manage stairs. Currently feels well at rest.
- Fever: Patient initially stated “fever,” but reported temperature 37°C and agreed it was normal (conflict noted).
- Past medical history: Childhood asthma (“quite bad”), hay fever, eczema. Occasional hospital visits for asthma in childhood; no ICU. Patient reports stopping asthma medication 3–4 years ago, but also reports “normally” using salbutamol every few weeks and with exercise (conflict noted).
- Medications: Salbutamol inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented); uses every few weeks and with exercise. No other regular meds.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Devices: No peak flow meter at home. No spacer.
- Social history: Nonsmoker. Alcohol ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days. Lives with partner. Works as an engineer; currently working from home/taking sick leave due to symptoms.
- Preventive care: Not discussed.

Examination:
- Vitals: Patient-reported temperature 37°C.
- Examination findings: Not performed (telemedicine).

Impression:
- Likely asthma exacerbation, possibly triggered by allergens/pollen or a viral infection.

Plan:
- Short-acting bronchodilator: Increase salbutamol to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours initially (use with a spacer).
- Prescriptions/devices: Provide spacer and peak flow meter; pharmacist to demonstrate use.
- Antihistamine: Begin regular over-the-counter antihistamine (specific agent not specified).
- Monitoring: Record peak flow values morning and evening for the next week.
- Safety net: Seek urgent advice if fever develops or wheeze/shortness of breath worsens.
- Follow-up: Arrange asthma review in 1 week (earlier if deterioration) to assess control and consider additional inhaler therapy.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Objective vitals (HR, RR, BP, O2 saturation); physical exam; peak flow baseline; detailed medication dosing/route/frequency; asthma action plan; trigger assessment; immunization status not discussed.
● Internal conflicts: Reported “fever” vs measured temp 37°C and described as normal. Reports stopping asthma meds 3–4 years ago vs “normally” using salbutamol every few weeks and with exercise.
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; some communication gaps and ambiguities leading to inconsistent history.
